Matthew 1: Jesus is born in the last years of Herod the Great, who died in 4 BC, so the birth is usually dated about 6–4 BC. The Gospel does not name its author; early tradition credits Matthew the tax collector (Matthew 9:9).
Matthew 2: Wise men come to Jerusalem "in the days of Herod the king" (Matthew 2:1). Joseph's family flees to Egypt and, after Herod's death, settles in Nazareth to avoid his son Archelaus, who ruled Judea until AD 6.
Matthew 3: John the Baptist preaches in the wilderness of Judea and baptizes in the Jordan, about AD 28 (Luke 3:1).
Matthew 4: After John is imprisoned, Jesus moves from Nazareth to Capernaum on the Sea of Galilee (Matthew 4:12–13), in the territory of Herod Antipas.
Matthew 5: Jesus teaches on a mountain in Galilee to crowds from Galilee, Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond Jordan (Matthew 4:25–5:1).
Matthew 6: The Sermon on the Mount continues, with teaching on alms, prayer, and fasting.
Matthew 7: The Sermon on the Mount ends, and "the people were astonished at his doctrine" (Matthew 7:28).
Matthew 8: Jesus heals in Capernaum, calms a storm, and crosses to the country of the Gergesenes on the east side of the lake.
Matthew 9: Back in "his own city" (Matthew 9:1), Capernaum, Jesus calls Matthew from the receipt of custom.
Matthew 10: Jesus sends out the twelve to "the lost sheep of the house of Israel" (Matthew 10:6), not to Gentiles or Samaritans.
Matthew 11: John the Baptist sends disciples from prison (Matthew 11:2). Josephus says Herod Antipas imprisoned John at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea.
Matthew 12: Jesus' disciples pick grain on the sabbath, and the Pharisees begin to plot against him.
Matthew 13: Jesus teaches parables from a boat by the sea, then is rejected in "his own country" (Matthew 13:54), Nazareth.
Matthew 14: Herod Antipas beheads John the Baptist at his birthday feast. Jesus withdraws to a desert place and feeds five thousand.
Matthew 15: Pharisees and scribes come from Jerusalem. Jesus goes to the coasts of Tyre and Sidon, Gentile territory to the northwest.
Matthew 16: At Caesarea Philippi, a city near the sources of the Jordan rebuilt by Herod's son Philip, Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ.
Matthew 17: Jesus is transfigured on "an high mountain" (Matthew 17:1) and pays the temple tax at Capernaum.
Matthew 18: Jesus teaches his disciples in Capernaum about greatness and forgiveness.
Matthew 19: Jesus leaves Galilee for "the coasts of Judaea beyond Jordan" (Matthew 19:1), on the way to Jerusalem.
Matthew 20: Jesus and the disciples go up toward Jerusalem and pass through Jericho.
Matthew 21: Jesus enters Jerusalem from Bethphage on the mount of Olives a few days before Passover, about AD 30 or 33, and cleanses the temple.
Matthew 22: In the temple courts, Pharisees and Herodians ask about tribute to Caesar, and Sadducees ask about the resurrection.
Matthew 23: Jesus speaks against the scribes and Pharisees and laments over Jerusalem.
Matthew 24: On the mount of Olives, opposite the temple, Jesus foretells its destruction. Rome destroyed the temple in AD 70.
Matthew 25: The teaching on the mount of Olives continues with the parables of the virgins, the talents, and the sheep and goats.
Matthew 26: Two days before Passover, Caiaphas, high priest AD 18–36, and the council plot Jesus' death. Jesus eats the Passover, prays in Gethsemane, and is arrested.
Matthew 27: Jesus is tried before Pontius Pilate, governor of Judea AD 26–36, and crucified at Golgotha. A stone inscription naming Pilate was found at Caesarea in 1961.
Matthew 28: On the first day of the week, the women find the tomb empty. The eleven meet Jesus on a mountain in Galilee.
Mark 1: Mark begins with John the Baptist in the wilderness and Jesus' early ministry in Capernaum. The Gospel does not name its author; early tradition (Papias) says Mark wrote down Peter's preaching.
Mark 2: Jesus is at home in Capernaum, calls Levi the tax collector, and is questioned about the sabbath.
Mark 3: Crowds come from Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumaea, beyond Jordan, and Tyre and Sidon (Mark 3:7–8). Jesus appoints the twelve.
Mark 4: Jesus teaches parables from a boat on the Sea of Galilee and calms a storm at night.
Mark 5: Jesus crosses to the country of the Gadarenes in the Decapolis, then returns to raise Jairus' daughter.
Mark 6: Jesus is rejected at Nazareth. Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee 4 BC–AD 39, has John beheaded.
Mark 7: Jesus goes to the borders of Tyre and Sidon and returns through the Decapolis (Mark 7:24, 31).
Mark 8: Jesus feeds four thousand, heals a blind man at Bethsaida, and asks his disciples at Caesarea Philippi who he is.
Mark 9: Jesus is transfigured and returns through Galilee to Capernaum.
Mark 10: Jesus goes into Judea by the far side of the Jordan and passes through Jericho, where Bartimaeus sits by the road.
Mark 11: Jesus enters Jerusalem from Bethphage and Bethany, curses a fig tree, and clears the temple court.
Mark 12: In the temple, Jesus answers the chief priests, Pharisees, Herodians, and Sadducees and watches a widow give two mites.
Mark 13: On the mount of Olives, opposite the temple, Jesus foretells the temple's destruction, which came in AD 70.
Mark 14: Two days before Passover, Jesus is anointed at Bethany. he eats the Passover, goes to Gethsemane, and is arrested.
Mark 15: Jesus is handed to Pilate in the morning and crucified at the third hour (Mark 15:25). Joseph of Arimathaea buries him before the sabbath.
Mark 16: Very early on the first day of the week, the women come to the tomb. The oldest manuscripts end at Mark 16:8.
